Cost = Users x Sessions/User x Turns/Session x Steps/Turn x Tokens/Step x Price/Token
Median 3 (Assignment 1), 4 (Assignment 2). Some turns run almost 1,000 steps, mostly because effort is set to medium or high.
Main agent median 208K (A1), 301K (A2); p90 600K-700K. Subagent median ~80K, p90 ~200K.
Adoption and engagement grow the first two factors. The agent trajectory and the unit price are the ones you can shrink.
Total cost grows with the square of the turn count.
Structured task decomposition, with a done check per subtask
The goal: finish autonomously, with no user check-ins.
One user turn expands into many steps, and every later turn pays for the earlier ones again.

slides.title: Steps: batch instead of one call per action

elements.text: Steps: batch instead of one call per action
Every model call re-reads the full context, so fewer calls cost less. Batch independent calls, reuse plans and skills, and load context up front.

slides.title: Tokens: shrink what enters, reduce what comes out

elements.text: TWO HALVES OF THE TOKEN BILL
Tokens: shrink what enters, reduce what comes out

Drop stale results
Compact history into state
Compress observations, keeping errors rather than full logs
Offload big outputs to files
Retrieve selectively
Isolate exploration in a sub-agent that returns a summary

Prompt-level constraints
Output-token caps
Structured output schemas
Adaptive reasoning effort
Adaptive reasoning effort: a lookup runs at effort="low", a debug runs at effort="high". Set it per call or per step, as a reasoning effort or a thinking-token budget.
Output constraints: "Answer in <= 100 words."  "Return only JSON."  "One sentence. Top 3 items." Caps are max_tokens=300 / max_output_tokens=300, but reasoning can use up the cap.
VOLUME AND PRICE POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS
Fresh prefill - 100x smaller than cache reads
Price ratio: cache read : input : output = 1 : 10 : 50
The most common token is the cheapest one: a cache read costs 1 against 10 for input and 50 for output.
of tokens in the measured usage were cache reads (Assignment 1)
Tokens that stay in context are paid for again on every later step.

NET SAVING IS WHAT YOU CAN CLAIM
net saving = gross saving - counter-cost. Measure both on the same tasks.

slides.title: Before you spend: does the step need reasoning?

elements.text: AND HOW THE TASK GETS BOUNDED
Before you spend: does the step need reasoning?
Check this before using an LLM at all
script the workflow, and call the LLM only at the steps that need it
Set limits from traced runs, e.g. 2x the p95 of successful tasks.
no new passing test appears in N steps
Then hand off with a summary: a stopped task with a summary costs less than a runaway one.

slides.title: Speed: completion time is the critical path

elements.text: NOT THE SUM OF EVERY STEP
Speed: completion time is the critical path
serial ~= the sum of the steps
Cheaper can be slower: small models may take more steps, and parallelism costs more tokens for less waiting.
every cost technique also cuts latency
async execution, persistent sessions, stream and pipeline, colocate services
cache tool results, faster hardware, better tools, fail fast - measure tool time per step first
the same work, a third of the wait
Latency is not just LLM latency: it is the critical path of the whole run.
PAY FOR THE WAIT, OR SPEND ONE WASTED CALL
A cheap model predicts the next action
It runs early, while the main model still thinks
A match skips the wait; a miss costs one wasted call
an early fork of the same model
It pays off when guesses are often right and actions can be undone. It can be lossless (always verify) or lossy.
SPORK example: think: 2,000 tokens ... early probe -> search(q)

Related work: Speculative Actions (ICLR 2026), Speculative Tool Calls (arXiv 2025), SPAgent (arXiv 2025), PASTE (arXiv 2026), B-PASTE (arXiv 2026), SPORK (arXiv 2026), Speculate with Memory (arXiv 2026), Speculative Macro Commit (arXiv 2026).
RESPONSIBILITY MOVING OUT OF THE AGENT
Everything in one runtime: the agent owns everything.
One controller delegates through interfaces. Providers: RedisMemory, MCPTools, SlidingWindowContext, DockerSandbox (Docker -> Firecracker swap).
Fit: swap the provider, not the agent.
The runtime keeps only state, coordination, scheduling and security; external services supply memory, tools and execution.

One Python snippet, three paths: monolithic executes locally, modular calls SandboxProvider.run(code), microkernel sends an execution request to an execution service that owns allocation, isolation and sandbox lifecycle.
The shift is from code, to interfaces, to services - and the microkernel trades simplicity and low overhead for isolation, sharing and scale.

slides.title: Eight real harnesses, one optimization loop

elements.text: Eight real harnesses, one optimization loop
Sandbox with no network access, approval only to go out of the sandbox; Lark patch grammar, hunks matched in four passes.
The loop is a plugin; compare-and-swap edits.
The harness is a server; nine replacers from exact to anchor match; a shadow git repository for /undo.
Core has four tools and no MCP; keep-alive requests only when the expected saving is $0.05 or more; pi-ai supports 42 providers on 10 wire APIs.
4-hex file tag plus line numbers per edit; one shell stays open for all calls; snapcompact changes old history into images; TTSR stops and tries again when a regex matches.
27 chat channels send messages to one lane for each session; memory before compaction; fences, taint and sentinels.
A background fork edits the memory and the skills; compaction starts at 50% of the window, the earliest of the eight; tool-call rows are written before any side effect.
The deck on the loop: "Remember this for your Assignment 4!"
Cost = Users x Sessions x Turns x Steps x Tokens x Price; only four of those factors are yours to shrink, and turns cost quadratically.
Every optimization has a counter-cost - measure net saving, not gross saving.
Better agents are not simply cheaper or faster; they are Pareto-efficient on capability, cost and speed.
This lecture focuses on LLM cost, and ignores the other compute costs.
Four factors are yours: turns, steps, tokens and price. The other two grow with adoption, and are not a lever.
A stable prefix is worth more than a shorter prompt.
